transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-01-23 16:00 UTC
Duration: 46 minutes (scheduled)
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Ravi Patel (Redwood SE), Linnea Gomez (Redwood Product), Carlos Ruiz (Horizon ML), Priya Menon (Horizon Platform), Dana Lee (CTO), Akira Sato (SRE)

Auto-generated summary (brief):
- Reviewed latest TTFT and streaming numbers from last pilot run; discussed surprising tail latency at longer sequences and streaming chunking behavior.
- Agreed to run kernel sweep (quantized vs fp16, fused attention variants) against customer trace.
- Action items assigned for artifacts and follow-ups (benchmarks, SOW, trace).

Topics: TTFT, streaming/partial-response chunking, sequence length regression, kernel selection, quantization tradeoffs, VPC/peering constraints, next-phase pilot scope.

Transcript:
[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for carving out time. Quick roll call — Maya from Redwood here, Ravi is with me, Linnea too. Carlos?
[00:07] Carlos Ruiz: Yep Carlos here. Sorry, had a calendar overlap, jumping in.
[00:10] Priya Menon: Priya here.
[00:12] Dana Lee: Dana on.
[00:13] Akira Sato: And Akira.
[00:15] Maya Chen: Great. The goal today is to go over the latest run notes — specifically TTFT and streaming behavior at 512 and 1k sequences, and pick a kernel/quantization plan for the next week. Ravi, quick high-level?
[00:29] Ravi Patel: Yeah, high level — we re-ran your pilot with two changes: enabled prefix KV caching for common prompts and switched to a 64ms batching window for streaming. We also tried int8 quant on the small model variant. The headline: median TTFT improved ~18% at seq512 but tail latency spiked at seq1024 with int8 on one of the kernels.
[00:48] Carlos Ruiz: When you say tail spiked, like p95/p99? Numbers?
[00:52] Ravi Patel: p95 moved from 210ms to 480ms on the NATIVE_FUSED kernel with int8 at seq1024. p99 went up to 920ms, looks like some kernel fallback or cache thrash. We saw similar but smaller increases on the cu-opt kernel — p95 around 350ms.
[01:12] Priya Menon: Hmm, that aligns with what we saw in prod traces last week — long prompts sometimes see a jittery tail, especially when multiple long requests come in simultaneously.
[01:22] Akira Sato: Do you think the KV cache eviction policy is interacting badly with int8? We run fairly bursty traffic.
[01:28] Ravi Patel: Possible — the int8 path is more memory-constrained so it can cause extra copies or fallbacks. Also, there was one observed error where the runtime recompiled a small kernel mid-run — noisy.
[01:37] Dana Lee: Recompiled? Is that expected in your hosted flows? We can't have mid-request recompiles in production.
[01:43] Ravi Patel: Not expected ideally. It's most common in dev kernels or when the fused kernel chooses a path incompatible with sequence length. We're seeing that on the NATIVE_FUSED int8 combo at long sequences.
[01:56] Maya Chen: Quick clarification — this test was on dedicated nodes or hosted?
[01:59] Ravi Patel: Dedicated testbed (4xA100-like config) but with the same runtime fuse flags as hosted. Different NUMA layout maybe contributing.
[02:07] Carlos Ruiz: Could you re-run without the 64ms streaming window just to isolate batching window vs kernel effect?
[02:12] Ravi Patel: Yeah we can. We already have a run queued that disables the streaming window (pure immediate stream) and also a run that keeps fp16 but toggles fused kernel versions. We'll prioritize the int8/fp16 A/B with the trace you promised, Carlos.
[02:25] Carlos Ruiz: I'll upload the trace after the call. Need to anonymize tokens but I can strip IDs.
[02:30] Priya Menon: Also on the network front — we noticed tail latency correlates with occasional retransmits between our load balancer and peered VPC. That might amplify any kernel stalls.
[02:40] Akira Sato: Right — we should replicate real network patterns during the benchmark. Can Redwood inject synthetic jitter?
[02:46] Ravi Patel: Yep, we can add a network jitter profile. We have a small harness to replay traces with configurable inter-request jitter and concurrency. Add that to the action list.
[02:55] Maya Chen: Good. Linnea, any product notes?
[02:58] Linnea Gomez: One thing — if we go with int8 for cost reasons we need to validate quality. We ran two eval prompt-sets and saw minor hallucination increases on a few templates; not catastrophic but we want to guard with quality monitoring and an automatic fallback to fp16 on regression.
[03:16] Dana Lee: Fallbacks are fine but we need SLOs — if quality drops beyond x% we must fallback within a minute. Also need an audit trail.
[03:24] Maya Chen: We have a rollout policy that can do canary + auto-fallback; we can tie it to your eval metrics. We'll send the docs.
[03:30] Carlos Ruiz: On the kernel side — what's realistic for you to test this week? We need p95 < 300ms for seq512 and burstable p99 < 700ms for seq1024, otherwise the UX regresses.
[03:43] Ravi Patel: For seq512 target we can probably hit p95 < 300ms with fp16 fused kernels and prefix caching. For seq1024, it's tougher — depends on whether the kernel falls back; int8 seems risky now. We'll run three experiments: (1) fp16 + fused, (2) fp16 + cu-opt, (3) int8 + cu-opt, all with KV caching. Also a fourth with no streaming window so we can see immediate vs batched streaming effects.
[04:06] Priya Menon: That sounds reasonable. For the experiment, can you output per-token timing and also include kernel fallback logs? We want visibility into where the runtime switches.
[04:15] Ravi Patel: Yes, we'll include per-token timeline logs and the runtime debug trace; note the debug trace includes long stack-like lines and may need log redaction.
[04:23] Carlos Ruiz: Fine. Maya, about security — do you have SOC2 + SAML docs we can share with our compliance team?
[04:29] Maya Chen: Yes, I'll attach a SOC2 summary and our SAML SSO integration guide after the call. Also short note on our VPC peering and private option.
[04:36] Dana Lee: And about VPC peering: Horizon's legal wants to know whether peering requires opening any egress, or if we can do a fully inbound-initiated connection.
[04:45] Maya Chen: Our typical peering allows mutual TLS and doesn't require broad egress; we can follow up with product network docs. If you need full on-prem, we also have a private deployment package.
[04:54] Akira Sato: What's the difference in latency profile if we move to Private (on-prem) vs Dedicated?
[04:59] Ravi Patel: Private on-prem eliminates cloud cross-tenant noisy neighbors but depends on your infra. Dedicated is similar if it's single-tenant GPU pools; the main differences are network topology and how quickly we can push kernel builds. On-prem gives you control but adds ops overhead.
[05:13] Carlos Ruiz: Let's assume dedicated for now; if network jitter persists we'll revisit.
[05:18] Maya Chen: Cool. Quick note on cost: int8 can reduce GPU memory and increase batch size which lowers unit cost, but the tail behavior we saw might increase overall cost due to retries/fallbacks. We'll include a cost delta in the spreadsheet.
[05:33] Priya Menon: For the streaming UX — the 64ms window improved median latency for small requests but increased TTFT for long sequences, is that right?
[05:41] Ravi Patel: Exactly. For short prompts, batching buys you token-efficiency and lower cost; for long sequences streaming immediate chunking avoids large initial wait but may reduce batching efficiency. It's a tradeoff.
[05:51] Dana Lee: Ops question — is there a per-request flag we can set to prefer low latency (no batching) vs cost-optimized? We want path-based policies.
[05:59] Linnea Gomez: Yes, you can set policy per route: low-latency mode disables batching and prefers fp16 fused kernels; cost mode allows int8 and bigger batch windows. We can surface this in the route config.
[06:12] Carlos Ruiz: Perfect. One more data ask: can you provide a matrix of kernel compatibility vs sequence length and quant mode? A simple table would help us pick defaults.
[06:22] Ravi Patel: We have an internal compatibility matrix — we'll export a trimmed version showing which kernels are stable per seq len and quant level. Add to deliverables.
[06:29] Maya Chen: OK, let's recap action items and owners. Ravi — kernel sweep + per-token logs + runtime trace with jitter profile, due 2026-01-27. Maya — send security and pricing docs by 2026-01-26. Carlos — upload anonymized trace by 2026-01-25. Priya — confirm peering requirement by 2026-01-29.
[06:49] Carlos Ruiz: Sounds good.
[06:51] Akira Sato: One small note — when you share the runtime trace, tag events where we see GC or memory pressure spikes; that'll help correlate.
[06:59] Ravi Patel: Will do.
[07:01] Dana Lee: Any blockers for the next run?
[07:04] Maya Chen: None from our side besides the trace upload.
[07:07] Priya Menon: We'll try to get the trace today. If not, earliest is Monday.
[07:12] Maya Chen: Alright, we'll plan a follow-up next week — 30 minutes — focused on the streaming TTFT numbers after the kernel sweep.
[07:19] Carlos Ruiz: Thanks all.
[07:21] Maya Chen: Thanks — we'll post the spreadsheet and SOW after the call.
[07:24] (call ends)
